title: Duality Theory for Filter Stability in Hidden Markov Models

paper.title:
Duality Theory for Filter Stability in Hidden Markov
Models Thanks: This work was funded by the AFOSR award

paper.abstract:
Abstract This article is concerned with the problem of nonlinear (stochastic) filter
stability for a discrete time hidden Markov model (HMM) with finite state and
observation spaces. For this purpose, a comprehensive duality theory is
developed whereby the dual control system is a backward stochastic difference
equation (BS Δ \Delta E). The duality is expressed in two inter-related forms.
In its variational form, the minimum mean squared error of optimal
filtering equals the value of a dual optimal control problem. In its structural form, controllability (resp. stabilizability) of the
BS Δ \Delta E and observability (resp. detectability) of the HMM are dual
properties. The dual optimal control problem supplies the Lyapunov function and the
dissipation: the former is the value function (a variance), the latter the
optimal running cost accumulated over the horizon. The main result is an
invariance principle: under any one of three model properties—ergodicity of
the Markov matrix, or observability or detectability of the HMM—zero
dissipation over a finite horizon forces the Lyapunov function to vanish. A
converse is also obtained: detectability is necessary. Two applications are given. The first is filter stability in χ 2 \chi^{2} -divergence: the invariance principle is applied in the manner of
LaSalle, to limits of trajectories along which the dissipation vanishes
asymptotically, the role of the model properties being to render the
zero-dissipation set trivial. The second is a quantitative form of the
invariance principle, through a Poincaré constant, from which convergence
rates follow. Both the model properties that govern stability and the
Lyapunov function that certifies it are thus obtained from a dual optimal
control problem, as in the classical theory for the linear Gaussian model.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: It has long been an aspiration to view estimation as a problem of optimal control, going back to Kalman’s work [ 27 ] . In the linear Gaussian setting, this connection is realized: both the model properties that govern stability of the Kalman filter and its Lyapunov function can be derived from a dual linear quadratic optimal control problem. Beyond the linear Gaussian model, the natural test of the duality is the problem of filter stability : whether the nonlinear filter forgets an incorrect prior. Whether Kalman’s duality extends to this setting, and if so in what form, is far from obvious. The aspiration has been taken up repeatedly—most notably in the minimum-energy dualities of Bryson–Frazier, Mortensen, and Hijab, and in their stochastic formulation by Fleming and Mitter and by Mitter and Newton [ 7 , 51 , 24 , 20 , 50 ] . These dualities, however, are not Kalman’s: their constraint is a copy of the signal model rather than the dual system, and detectability does not arise as the dual of stabilizability [ 5 , Sec. 7.3.1 and 7.3.2] . Todorov concluded that Kalman’s duality does not extend beyond the linear Gaussian setting [ 61 ] . Van Handel similarly observed, in his survey of nonlinear filter stability, that proofs of nonlinear filter stability must “start from scratch” [ 65 ] . Yet the possibility of a deeper connection was recognized. In his PhD thesis, van Handel listed the connections between filter stability and stochastic control as meriting further investigation, observing that the relationship, in the linear case, between filter stability and controllability and observability [ 52 ] “makes it tempting to look for such connections in the nonlinear case” [ 62 , p. 17] . The suggestion remained a direction for future work. The subsequent development of observability and detectability for nonlinear filters, and the stability proofs based on them, proceeded instead by probabilistic methods [ 63 , 64 , 13 , 65 ] , now known as the intrinsic approach to filter stability. At a minimum, a duality theory should do for the nonlinear filter what it does for the Kalman filter: (a) identify the model properties that govern stability, and (b) provide a Lyapunov function that certifies it. For the hidden Markov model (HMM) in its basic form—discrete time with finite state and observation spaces—this paper does exactly that: both the model properties and the Lyapunov function are derived from a dual optimal control problem. The focus on the finite-state discrete-time HMM is motivated by two considerations. First, it is the simplest setting in which the essential difficulties of nonlinear filtering already appear: even for an ergodic finite-state chain, the filter need not forget an incorrect prior (Example 1 , due to Kaijser [ 26 ] ). It is therefore the natural setting in which the duality theory should first be understood, free of the technical overhead of the general case. Second, it is the standard model for reinforcement learning in partially observed Markov decision processes (POMDPs). There, filter stability is a key ingredient in learning near-optimal policies from a finite window of past observations [ 30 , 29 ] , and in bounding the loss incurred by controlling with an incorrect prior [ 47 ] .

sections.heading: 1.1 Approach and contributions of this paper
sections.text: While the intrinsic approach is based on the forward map γ 0 ↦ γ T \gamma_{0}\mapsto\gamma_{T} between the Radon–Nikodym derivatives at time t = 0 t=0 and t = T t=T (Sec. 2.3 ), the dual approach of this paper is based on a backward map γ T ↦ y 0 \gamma_{T}\mapsto y_{0} (Eq. ( 3 )). Filter stability in the sense of χ 2 \chi^{2} -divergence follows from a variance decay property of the backward map (Prop. 10 ). To show this property, the backward map is embedded in a backward process (Eq. ( 4 )), which is the solution of the dual optimal control system. The contributions are as follows. 1. The main result is an invariance principle , Lemma 12 , for the backward process. The principle relates the model properties that govern stability and the Lyapunov function that certifies it. (a) The three model properties are ergodicity of the Markov matrix, and observability and detectability of the HMM, the first and third under a non-degeneracy condition on the emission matrix (Assumption 2 ). (b) The Lyapunov function is the variance of a backward process (Prop. 11 ). It is non-increasing in the backward direction of time, and the dissipation—the amount by which it decreases—is identified explicitly, as the running cost of the dual optimal control problem. Filter stability follows if the Lyapunov function at the initial time decays to zero as T → ∞ T\to\infty . The invariance principle is the statement that, under any one of the three model properties, zero dissipation over a finite horizon forces zero variance. Conversely, if this implication holds for every horizon, prior, and terminal condition, then the HMM is detectable (Prop. 25 ). Therefore, detectability is necessary for the invariance principle to hold in this generality. 2. Duality theory for the HMM . The dual control system is a backward stochastic difference equation (BS Δ \Delta E). As in the classical setting, duality is expressed in two inter-related manners: (i) Variational (minimum-variance) duality : Prop. 22 and Cor. 23 show that the minimum mean squared error (MMSE) of optimal filtering equals the value of the dual optimal control problem. Moreover, it identifies the Lyapunov function with that value function. (ii) Structural duality : Prop. 21 shows that controllability (resp. stabilizability) of the BS Δ \Delta E and observability (resp. detectability) of HMM are dual properties. The development parallels linear systems theory throughout: the controllable subspace, its recursion, the stabilization index, and the annihilator pairing with the nonobservable subspace all appear in their familiar form. 3. Filter stability (Thm. 27 ). Assuming equivalent priors and any one of the three model properties, the filter is stable in χ 2 \chi^{2} -divergence. The proof is a stability argument in the classical sense: The invariance principle (Lemma 12 ) is applied in the manner of LaSalle, to limits of trajectories along which dissipation vanishes asymptotically. The role of model properties is to render the zero-dissipation set trivial. 4. Rates . The conclusion of Lemma 12 is made quantitative through a Poincaré constant κ ⁡ ( ρ ) \kappa(\rho) (Defn. 32 ). This yields a decay bound along the filter’s own trajectory (Prop. 36 ) and a dichotomy (Thm. 37 ): either the filter is stable in χ 2 \chi^{2} -divergence, or its skeleton converges to the set on which κ \kappa degenerates.

sections.heading: 1.2 Literature
sections.text: For the linear Gaussian model, filter stability is classical, and is understood through Kalman’s duality between filtering and control [ 28 ] , [ 41 , Sec. 4.4] , [ 52 , Sec. 2] . The model property for stability of the Kalman filter is detectability of the linear Gaussian model, which by an elementary duality is equivalent to stabilizability of the dual control system. A standard proof technique for the asymptotic convergence of the Kalman filter error covariance is based on the dual linear quadratic (LQ) problem: a stabilizing control bounds the cost uniformly in time, and the value function serves as a Lyapunov function [ 52 , Lemma 2.2] , [ 66 , Ch. 9] , [ 6 , Proof of Thm. 23.2] . These optimal control foundations extend far beyond the LQ case, and without them it is difficult to imagine the modern stability theory for deterministic nonlinear systems. Input-to-state stability (ISS) has its roots in dissipativity theory, with general (non-positive-definite) running costs [ 55 ] , and the dual notion of detectability [ 56 ] is central to the stability of model predictive control [ 21 , 22 ] . A primary motivation for introducing incremental input/output-to-state stability (i-IOSS) is its use in deducing the asymptotic stability of the minimum-energy estimator (MEE) [ 40 ] , [ 53 , Defn. 4.1 and Prop. 4.9] . No comparable theory exists for the nonlinear filter—one in which both the model properties and the Lyapunov function come from a dual control problem. The literature on nonlinear filter stability distinguishes two cases [ 11 , 13 ] : (i) The ergodic signal case , where the hidden Markov process forgets its initial condition and the filter inherits the property. (ii) The nonergodic signal case , where the observations provide enough information about the hidden state for the filter to correct an erroneous prior. For the ergodic signal case, early work is based on contraction analysis of the random matrix products that arise from recursive application of Bayes’ formula [ 3 , 43 , 44 ] , [ 8 , Sec. 4.3] , [ 15 , 17 ] , and, for the Zakai equation, on formulae for the Lyapunov exponents [ 2 , 1 , 4 ] . The analysis requires a non-degeneracy assumption (Assumption 2 ), satisfied by the white noise observations; without it, the filter need not be stable even when the signal is ergodic [ 26 , 16 ] (see Example 1 ). For the nonergodic signal case, notable early contributions are [ 14 ] , where the relative entropy is shown to be a Lyapunov function for the filter, and [ 12 ] , where the filter is shown to be stable for functions that predict the observations. For a class of diffusions, filter stability results of this type are obtained by PDE methods in [ 57 , 58 ] . Definitions of observability and detectability, and their relationship to filter stability, first appear in [ 63 , 64 ] . In both cases the proofs directly exploit the representation of the filter as a conditional expectation, through classical probabilistic techniques—the intrinsic approach [ 13 ] . McDonald and Yüksel [ 46 , 48 ] introduce a different, explicitly stated notion of observability for nonlinear systems, and show that it yields stability of the predictor, with filter stability following under additional conditions. They also establish a set of implications among the stability criteria themselves—weak merging, total variation merging, and merging in relative entropy—which complements the relative entropy bounds of [ 14 ] . This paper builds on our prior work [ 38 , 35 , 36 ] , where duality for nonlinear filtering was first introduced for the continuous-time HMM with white noise observations. In this prior work, a backward stochastic differential equation (BSDE) was introduced as the dual control system, and observability of the HMM and controllability of the BSDE were shown to be dual properties [ 35 , 32 ] . The use of this duality to prove filter stability was begun in [ 39 , 34 , 37 , 33 ] , based on a backward map and a variance decay property, both of which are central here as well, but stability results were possible only in special cases [ 37 , Thm. 3] . Relative to our prior work, the contributions of the present paper are the following. Our previous results were limited to white noise observations, while the present work concerns the HMM in settings of most practical relevance. In some ways, duality theory for the finite setting is easier, being based entirely on linear algebra, which also makes the connection to Kalman’s duality transparent. In other ways it is more delicate, requiring careful track of the time horizons: those for the three model properties, and the horizon at which the Poincaré constant is evaluated. These have no counterpart in continuous time. Apart from these differences, the following are novel contributions of this paper: 1. The main result—the invariance principle (Lemma 12 )—is new. So is its converse (Prop. 25 ). 2. The proof of filter stability is new. To the best of our knowledge, the proof given here is the first variational, or control-theoretic, proof of nonlinear filter stability under conditions on the model alone (Thm. 27 ). 3. The regularity theory for the Poincaré constant is new. The analysis of the constant as a function on the probability simplex is new (Prop. 34 and Lemma 35 ). It is fair to ask what is gained, given that the intrinsic approach has settled filter stability under necessary and sufficient conditions. Our answer: 1. The finite setting is treated comprehensively. The three model properties reduce to conditions of linear algebra, as transparent as in the linear case, and the indices that mark the horizons at which they take effect are identified explicitly. One of these is related to the classical index of primitivity [ 44 ] ; the other two, and the role of the indices in filter stability, appear to be new. 2. The model properties for stability are not assumed but derived. Asking what is required for the variance to decay, the theory returns stabilizability of the dual control system, and the converse (Prop. 25 ) shows that stabilizability is also necessary. 3. The same theory delivers the rates, through the Poincaré constant, which for a given model is computed by solving a finite-dimensional eigenvalue problem. This makes the theory useful in practice and informs the future work. We close by returning to the aspiration with which we began. For the finite-state HMM the answer is affirmative: Kalman’s duality does extend to the purposes of filter stability, and it extends in both respects—it identifies the properties of the model responsible for stability, and it supplies the Lyapunov function with which stability is proved.

sections.heading: 1.3 Paper outline
sections.text: Sec. 2 contains mathematical preliminaries. Sec. 3 introduces the backward map and states the main result (Lemma 12 ). Sec. 4 presents a proof of the main result for the ergodic case. Sec. 5 develops the duality theory for the HMM, which is used in Sec. 6 to prove the main result for the observable and detectable cases, and to establish its converse. The main result is applied in Sec. 7 to prove filter stability, and in Sec. 8 to derive rates. The appendices contain the technical proofs. A reader may wish to review Defn. 1 of γ T \gamma_{T} and Defn. 8 of ℨ T ∘ ​ ( ρ ) \mathfrak{Z}^{\circ}_{T}(\rho) , and then proceed to Sec. 3 , returning to Sec. 2 as needed. sections.heading: 5 Duality theory for HMM
sections.text: The framework described in this section generalizes the classical duality theory for linear time-invariant systems. 1. Structural duality . For the HMM, we have already introduced the notions of observability and detectability (Sec. 2.5 ). The dual notions are presented in Sec. 5.1 . 2. Variational duality . The foundational link between optimal filtering and optimal control is the duality principle presented in Sec. 5.2 . This is followed by the formulation and solution of the dual optimal control problem in Sec. 5.3 . The presentation closely mirrors that of linear systems theory.

Prashant G. Mehta † † thanks: Coordinated Science Laboratory, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL (, https://mehta.mechse.illinois.edu/ ). Email: mehtapg@illinois.edu Abstract This article is concerned with the problem of nonlinear (stochastic) filter stability for a discrete time hidden Markov model (HMM) with finite state and observation spaces. For this purpose, a comprehensive duality theory is developed whereby the dual control system is a backward stochastic difference equation (BS Δ \Delta E). The duality is expressed in two inter-related forms. In its variational form, the minimum mean squared error of optimal filtering equals the value of a dual optimal control problem. In its structural form, controllability (resp. stabilizability) of the BS Δ \Delta E and observability (resp. detectability) of the HMM are dual properties. The dual optimal control problem supplies the Lyapunov function and the dissipation: the former is the value function (a variance), the latter the optimal running cost accumulated over the horizon. The main result is an invariance principle: under any one of three model properties—ergodicity of the Markov matrix, or observability or detectability of the HMM—zero dissipation over a finite horizon forces the Lyapunov function to vanish. A converse is also obtained: detectability is necessary. Two applications are given. The first is filter stability in χ 2 \chi^{2} -divergence: the invariance principle is applied in the manner of LaSalle, to limits of trajectories along which the dissipation vanishes asymptotically, the role of the model properties being to render the zero-dissipation set trivial. The second is a quantitative form of the invariance principle, through a Poincaré constant, from which convergence rates follow. Both the model properties that govern stability and the Lyapunov function that certifies it are thus obtained from a dual optimal control problem, as in the classical theory for the linear Gaussian model. keywords nonlinear filtering, filter stability, hidden Markov model, duality, observability, detectability, backward stochastic difference equation, Poincaré inequality. † † runningheads: Duality Theory for Filter Stability / P. G. Mehta MSC 93E11, 93E15, 93E20, 93B07, 93B05, 60J10. 1 Introduction It has long been an aspiration to view estimation as a problem of optimal control, going back to Kalman’s work [ 27 ] . In the linear Gaussian setting, this connection is realized: both the model properties that govern stability of the Kalman filter and its Lyapunov function can be derived from a dual linear quadratic optimal control problem. Beyond the linear Gaussian model, the natural test of the duality is the problem of filter stability : whether the nonlinear filter forgets an incorrect prior. Whether Kalman’s duality extends to this setting, and if so in what form, is far from obvious. The aspiration has been taken up repeatedly—most notably in the minimum-energy dualities of Bryson–Frazier, Mortensen, and Hijab, and in their stochastic formulation by Fleming and Mitter and by Mitter and Newton [ 7 , 51 , 24 , 20 , 50 ] . These dualities, however, are not Kalman’s: their constraint is a copy of the signal model rather than the dual system, and detectability does not arise as the dual of stabilizability [ 5 , Sec. 7.3.1 and 7.3.2] . Todorov concluded that Kalman’s duality does not extend beyond the linear Gaussian setting [ 61 ] . Van Handel similarly observed, in his survey of nonlinear filter stability, that proofs of nonlinear filter stability must “start from scratch” [ 65 ] . Yet the possibility of a deeper connection was recognized. In his PhD thesis, van Handel listed the connections between filter stability and stochastic control as meriting further investigation, observing that the relationship, in the linear case, between filter stability and controllability and observability [ 52 ] “makes it tempting to look for such connections in the nonlinear case” [ 62 , p. 17] . The suggestion remained a direction for future work. The subsequent development of observability and detectability for nonlinear filters, and the stability proofs based on them, proceeded instead by probabilistic methods [ 63 , 64 , 13 , 65 ] , now known as the intrinsic approach to filter stability. At a minimum, a duality theory should do for the nonlinear filter what it does for the Kalman filter: (a) identify the model properties that govern stability, and (b) provide a Lyapunov function that certifies it. For the hidden Markov model (HMM) in its basic form—discrete time with finite state and observation spaces—this paper does exactly that: both the model properties and the Lyapunov function are derived from a dual optimal control problem. The focus on the finite-state discrete-time HMM is motivated by two considerations. First, it is the simplest setting in which the essential difficulties of nonlinear filtering already appear: even for an ergodic finite-state chain, the filter need not forget an incorrect prior (Example 1 , due to Kaijser [ 26 ] ). It is therefore the natural setting in which the duality theory should first be understood, free of the technical overhead of the general case. Second, it is the standard model for reinforcement learning in partially observed Markov decision processes (POMDPs). There, filter stability is a key ingredient in learning near-optimal policies from a finite window of past observations [ 30 , 29 ] , and in bounding the loss incurred by controlling with an incorrect prior [ 47 ] . 1.1 Approach and contributions of this paper While the intrinsic approach is based on the forward map γ 0 ↦ γ T \gamma_{0}\mapsto\gamma_{T} between the Radon–Nikodym derivatives at time t = 0 t=0 and t = T t=T (Sec. 2.3 ), the dual approach of this paper is based on a backward map γ T ↦ y 0 \gamma_{T}\mapsto y_{0} (Eq. ( 3 )). Filter stability in the sense of χ 2 \chi^{2} -divergence follows from a variance decay property of the backward map (Prop. 10 ). To show this property, the backward map is embedded in a backward process (Eq. ( 4 )), which is the solution of the dual optimal control system. The contributions are as follows. 1. The main result is an invariance principle , Lemma 12 , for the backward process. The principle relates the model properties that govern stability and the Lyapunov function that certifies it. (a) The three model properties are ergodicity of the Markov matrix, and observability and detectability of the HMM, the first and third under a non-degeneracy condition on the emission matrix (Assumption 2 ). (b) The Lyapunov function is the variance of a backward process (Prop. 11 ). It is non-increasing in the backward direction of time, and the dissipation—the amount by which it decreases—is identified explicitly, as the running cost of the dual optimal control problem. Filter stability follows if the Lyapunov function at the initial time decays to zero as T → ∞ T\to\infty . The invariance principle is the statement that, under any one of the three model properties, zero dissipation over a finite horizon forces zero variance. Conversely, if this implication holds for every horizon, prior, and terminal condition, then the HMM is detectable (Prop. 25 ). Therefore, detectability is necessary for the invariance principle to hold in this generality. 2. Duality theory for the HMM . The dual control system is a backward stochastic difference equation (BS Δ \Delta E). As in the classical setting, duality is expressed in two inter-related manners: (i) Variational (minimum-variance) duality : Prop. 22 and Cor. 23 show that the minimum mean squared error (MMSE) of optimal filtering equals the value of the dual optimal control problem. Moreover, it identifies the Lyapunov function with that value function. (ii) Structural duality : Prop. 21 shows that controllability (resp. stabilizability) of the BS Δ \Delta E and observability (resp. detectability) of HMM are dual properties. The development parallels linear systems theory throughout: the controllable subspace, its recursion, the stabilization index, and the annihilator pairing with the nonobservable subspace all appear in their familiar form. 3. Filter stability (Thm. 27 ). Assuming equivalent priors and any one of the three model properties, the filter is stable in χ 2 \chi^{2} -divergence. The proof is a stability argument in the classical sense: The invariance principle (Lemma 12 ) is applied in the manner of LaSalle, to limits of trajectories along which dissipation vanishes asymptotically. The role of model properties is to render the zero-dissipation set trivial. 4. Rates . The conclusion of Lemma 12 is made quantitative through a Poincaré constant κ ⁡ ( ρ ) \kappa(\rho) (Defn. 32 ). This yields a decay bound along the filter’s own trajectory (Prop. 36 ) and a dichotomy (Thm. 37 ): either the filter is stable in χ 2 \chi^{2} -divergence, or its skeleton converges to the set on which κ \kappa degenerates. 1.2 Literature For the linear Gaussian model, filter stability is classical, and is understood through Kalman’s duality between filtering and control [ 28 ] , [ 41 , Sec. 4.4] , [ 52 , Sec. 2] . The model property for stability of the Kalman filter is detectability of the linear Gaussian model, which by an elementary duality is equivalent to stabilizability of the dual control system. A standard proof technique for the asymptotic convergence of the Kalman filter error covariance is based on the dual linear quadratic (LQ) problem: a stabilizing control bounds the cost uniformly in time, and the value function serves as a Lyapunov function [ 52 , Lemma 2.2] , [ 66 , Ch. 9] , [ 6 , Proof of Thm. 23.2] . These optimal control foundations extend far beyond the LQ case, and without them it is difficult to imagine the modern stability theory for deterministic nonlinear systems. Input-to-state stability (ISS) has its roots in dissipativity theory, with general (non-positive-definite) running costs [ 55 ] , and the dual notion of detectability [ 56 ] is central to the stability of model predictive control [ 21 , 22 ] . A primary motivation for introducing incremental input/output-to-state stability (i-IOSS) is its use in deducing the asymptotic stability of the minimum-energy estimator (MEE) [ 40 ] , [ 53 , Defn. 4.1 and Prop. 4.9] . No comparable theory exists for the nonlinear filter—one in which both the model properties and the Lyapunov function come from a dual control problem. The literature on nonlinear filter stability distinguishes two cases [ 11 , 13 ] : (i) The ergodic signal case , where the hidden Markov process forgets its initial condition and the filter inherits the property. (ii) The nonergodic signal case , where the observations provide enough information about the hidden state for the filter to correct an erroneous prior. For the ergodic signal case, early work is based on contraction analysis of the random matrix products that arise from recursive application of Bayes’ formula [ 3 , 43 , 44 ] , [ 8 , Sec. 4.3] , [ 15 , 17 ] , and, for the Zakai equation, on formulae for the Lyapunov exponents [ 2 , 1 , 4 ] . The analysis requires a non-degeneracy assumption (Assumption 2 ), satisfied by the white noise observations; without it, the filter need not be stable even when the signal is ergodic [ 26 , 16 ] (see Example 1 ). For the nonergodic signal case, notable early contributions are [ 14 ] , where the relative entropy is shown to be a Lyapunov function for the filter, and [ 12 ] , where the filter is shown to be stable for functions that predict the observations. For a class of diffusions, filter stability results of this type are obtained by PDE methods in [ 57 , 58 ] . Definitions of observability and detectability, and their relationship to filter stability, first appear in [ 63 , 64 ] . In both cases the proofs directly exploit the representation of the filter as a conditional expectation, through classical probabilistic techniques—the intrinsic approach [ 13 ] . McDonald and Yüksel [ 46 , 48 ] introduce a different, explicitly stated notion of observability for nonlinear systems, and show that it yields stability of the predictor, with filter stability following under additional conditions. They also establish a set of implications among the stability criteria themselves—weak merging, total variation merging, and merging in relative entropy—which complements the relative entropy bounds of [ 14 ] . This paper builds on our prior work [ 38 , 35 , 36 ] , where duality for nonlinear filtering was first introduced for the continuous-time HMM with white noise observations. In this prior work, a backward stochastic differential equation (BSDE) was introduced as the dual control system, and observability of the HMM and controllability of the BSDE were shown to be dual properties [ 35 , 32 ] . The use of this duality to prove filter stability was begun in [ 39 , 34 , 37 , 33 ] , based on a backward map and a variance decay property, both of which are central here as well, but stability results were possible only in special cases [ 37 , Thm. 3] . Relative to our prior work, the contributions of the present paper are the following. Our previous results were limited to white noise observations, while the present work concerns the HMM in settings of most practical relevance. In some ways, duality theory for the finite setting is easier, being based entirely on linear algebra, which also makes the connection to Kalman’s duality transparent. In other ways it is more delicate, requiring careful track of the time horizons: those for the three model properties, and the horizon at which the Poincaré constant is evaluated. These have no counterpart in continuous time. Apart from these differences, the following are novel contributions of this paper: 1. The main result—the invariance principle (Lemma 12 )—is new. So is its converse (Prop. 25 ). 2. The proof of filter stability is new. To the best of our knowledge, the proof given here is the first variational, or control-theoretic, proof of nonlinear filter stability under conditions on the model alone (Thm. 27 ). 3. The regularity theory for the Poincaré constant is new. The analysis of the constant as a function on the probability simplex is new (Prop. 34 and Lemma 35 ). It is fair to ask what is gained, given that the intrinsic approach has settled filter stability under necessary and sufficient conditions. Our answer: 1. The finite setting is treated comprehensively. The three model properties reduce to conditions of linear algebra, as transparent as in the linear case, and the indices that mark the horizons at which they take effect are identified explicitly. One of these is related to the classical index of primitivity [ 44 ] ; the other two, and the role of the indices in filter stability, appear to be new. 2. The model properties for stability are not assumed but derived. Asking what is required for the variance to decay, the theory returns stabilizability of the dual control system, and the converse (Prop. 25 ) shows that stabilizability is also necessary. 3. The same theory delivers the rates, through the Poincaré constant, which for a given model is computed by solving a finite-dimensional eigenvalue problem. This makes the theory useful in practice and informs the future work. We close by returning to the aspiration with which we began. For the finite-state HMM the answer is affirmative: Kalman’s duality does extend to the purposes of filter stability, and it extends in both respects—it identifies the properties of the model responsible for stability, and it supplies the Lyapunov function with which stability is proved. 1.3 Paper outline Sec. 2 contains mathematical preliminaries. Sec. 3 introduces the backward map and states the main result (Lemma 12 ). Sec. 4 presents a proof of the main result for the ergodic case. Sec. 5 develops the duality theory for the HMM, which is used in Sec. 6 to prove the main result for the observable and detectable cases, and to establish its converse. The main result is applied in Sec. 7 to prove filter stability, and in Sec. 8 to derive rates. The appendices contain the technical proofs.
